input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-344: Programming Language Concepts. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course is a study of the syntax and semantics of a diverse set of high-level programming languages. The languages chosen are compared and contrasted in order to demonstrate general principles of programming language design and implementation. The course emphasizes the concepts underpinning modern languages rather than the mastery of particular language details. Programming projects will be required. Prerequisites: CSCI-243 or SWEN-250 or IGME-309 or 4003-334 or 4010-361 or 4080-487) and (MATH-190 or MATH-200) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer Regeneration revision 2: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label.

Source excerpts:

[llvm-language-reference]
LLVM IR is a typed, SSA-based intermediate representation with explicit instructions, basic blocks, functions, memory operations, and control flow. A module contains global values, functions, declarations, and metadata. A function contains basic blocks, and every basic block ends with a terminator instruction. Phi instructions select values according to the predecessor control-flow edge. Load and store instructions make memory access explicit. Valid IR must satisfy structural and typing rules. The verifier reports IR that violates those rules. Compiler work separates parsing and semantic analysis from lowering, verification, optimization, and target-specific code generation.

[python-language-reference]
The Python language reference specifies lexical analysis, data model behavior, execution, expressions, statements, functions, classes, exceptions, and module import semantics. Python objects have identity, a type, and a value. Names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes. Expressions produce values, while statements control execution and bindings. Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate. The import system searches for modules and binds loaded modules into a namespace. Programs should be reasoned about through explicit state, control flow, data representation, contracts, tests, and observable behavior. Debugging separates syntax, runtime, and logical failures, while decomposition and abstraction reduce the number of interacting concerns.

The course emphasizes the concepts underpinning modern languages rather than the mastery of particular language details. Programming projects will be required. Prerequisites: CSCI-243 or SWEN-250 or IGME-309 or 4003-334 or 4010-361 or 4080-487) and (MATH-190 or MATH-200) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

beats.claim: A programming language specification organizes code into modules containing global values, functions, and metadata that define the program's overall structure.
beats.example: An LLVM module groups all global variables, function definitions, and type declarations into a single unit before compilation begins.
beats.title: Module Structure and IR Representation
beats.visualDirection: Display a hierarchical diagram showing a module node branching into global values, function nodes, and metadata nodes, with clear labels for each component.

beats.claim: Functions are divided into basic blocks that execute sequentially until a terminator instruction redirects execution to a specific predecessor control-flow edge.
beats.example: A conditional branch in a function splits into two basic blocks, each terminating with a jump instruction that routes to the next logical step.
beats.title: Basic Blocks and Control Flow
beats.visualDirection: Render a flowchart of a function with three basic blocks, highlighting the terminator instruction at the end of each block and arrows indicating control flow paths.

beats.claim: Phi instructions select values according to the predecessor control-flow edge, enabling correct variable state tracking across merged execution paths.
beats.example: When two branches converge, a phi instruction chooses the value from the branch that was actually executed during runtime.
beats.title: Phi Instructions and Value Selection
beats.visualDirection: Show a diamond-shaped control flow graph with a phi node at the merge point, labeled with the values from each incoming edge.

beats.claim: Load and store instructions make memory access explicit, requiring the compiler to track where data is read from and written to in the program's address space.
beats.example: A store instruction assigns a computed value to a specific memory location, while a load instruction retrieves that value for further computation.
beats.title: Explicit Memory Operations
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a memory model with a register, a memory address, and arrows showing a store writing to memory and a load reading from it.

beats.claim: Valid IR must satisfy structural and typing rules, and the verifier reports IR that violates those rules to catch errors before optimization begins.
beats.example: The verifier checks that every basic block ends with a terminator and that all variables are properly typed before the compiler proceeds.
beats.title: Structural Verification Rules
beats.visualDirection: Display a checklist graphic with three boxes: structural rules, typing rules, and verifier output, showing a red 'X' on a rule violation.

beats.claim: Compiler work separates parsing and semantic analysis from lowering, verification, optimization, and target-specific code generation, allowing each phase to focus on distinct tasks
beats.example: The parser converts source code into an abstract syntax tree, while the semantic analyzer checks types and scopes before the lowering phase begins.
beats.title: Compiler Work Separation
beats.visualDirection: Draw a linear pipeline diagram with five stages labeled parsing, semantic analysis, lowering, verification, optimization, and code generation, with arrows flowing left to right.

beats.claim: Names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes, and lexical analysis breaks source code into tokens that define the program's lexical structure.
beats.example: A variable declared inside a function belongs to the function's local scope, while a global variable is bound to the module's namespace.
beats.title: Lexical Analysis and Scoping
beats.visualDirection: Show nested boxes representing global and local scopes, with variable names placed inside the appropriate scope box and arrows indicating binding relationships.

beats.claim: Python objects have identity, a type, and a value, and the execution model processes expressions to produce values while statements control execution and bindings.
beats.example: An integer object has a unique memory address, a type tag, and a numeric value, while an assignment statement binds a name to that object.
beats.title: Data Model and Execution Model
beats.visualDirection: Render a simple object diagram showing an object with three fields: identity (address), type, and value, alongside an assignment arrow binding a name to it.

beats.claim: Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate, allowing programs to handle errors without halting execution.
beats.example: When a division by zero occurs, an exception jumps out of the current block and is caught by a try-except handler that logs the error and continues.
beats.title: Exception Handling and Control Flow
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a control flow path with a normal execution line, a red 'exception' arrow jumping to a handler block, and a green 'propagate' arrow moving upward.

beats.claim: Debugging separates syntax, runtime, and logical failures, while decomposition and abstraction reduce the number of interacting concerns to simplify program analysis.
beats.example: A syntax error is caught by the parser, a runtime error occurs during execution, and a logical error is fixed by breaking the code into smaller, testable functions.
beats.title: Debugging and Decomposition
beats.visualDirection: Show a three-column table labeled syntax, runtime, and logical failures, with each column containing a brief example and a corresponding debugging tool icon.

learningObjectives: Define the core components of a programming language specification, including syntax, semantics, and execution model.
Explain how lexical analysis, scoping, and data model behavior govern program execution and state management.
Apply structural verification and debugging methodologies to identify and resolve syntactic, runtime, and logical errors in code.

With the foundation in place, examine how Phi Instructions and Value Selection operates in a concrete sequence. Phi instructions select values according to the predecessor control-flow edge. Consider this worked case: When two branches converge, a phi instruction chooses the value from the branch that was actually executed during runtime.
